subtitle.en: Giving your point of view and backing it up
subtitle.tx: O'z nuqtai nazarini bildirish va asoslash

body.en: Uzbek has no word like “that” to open a clause, and no special verb mood for opinions. The easiest way to give an opinion is menimcha (“in my opinion”) + an ordinary sentence: Menimcha, u ertaga keladi = I think he'll come tomorrow. To put a whole clause inside a sentence, Uzbek either quotes it and closes it with deb (“saying”): «Keladi», deb o'ylayman = I think he'll come; or turns the verb into a noun with -ish / -gan + a possessive and a case ending: U kelishini o'ylayman = I think he'll come; Yaxshi ekaningizga umid qilaman = I hope you are well.

To say “even though / although”, add ham to the conditional -sa: Charchagan bo'lsam ham, ishladim = Even though I was tired, I worked. With a noun or an adjective use bo'lsa ham: Kech bo'lsa ham = even though it was late. The -sa ham clause comes first and the main clause follows.

examples: Even though I was tired, I worked.
Even though it was late, we went out.

body.en: Useful words for building an argument: birinchidan (firstly), bundan tashqari (besides), shunga qaramay (nevertheless), demak (so, therefore), chunki (because), natijada (as a result). They usually open the sentence and are followed by a comma.

subtitle.en: Telling complex events, memories and anecdotes

body.en: For an action that happened before another past action, Uzbek uses -gan + edi, with the personal ending on edi: Men kelganimda, u ketgan edi = When I arrived, he had already left. It works like the English “had done”, and allaqachon (already) often goes with it.

ekan marks information you heard from someone else or have just found out, rather than seen yourself: U kelmas ekan = Apparently he isn't coming. English needs a word like apparently, it turns out or it seems; Uzbek just adds ekan after the verb. It is very common in everyday speech.

Useful endings and words for telling a story: -gach (after, once), -guncha (until), -dan keyin (after), -ganda / -ayotganda (when, while), birdan (suddenly), o'sha paytda (at that moment). They attach to the verb, so “after I arrived” is a single word plus keyin: kelganimdan keyin.

body.en: Uzbek makes a verb passive by adding -il- to the stem (-l- after a vowel): yozmoq (to write) → yozilmoq (to be written). When the stem ends in l or in -la, the suffix becomes -(i)n-: olmoq → olinmoq, imzolamoq (to sign) → imzolanmoq (to be signed). The doer is usually left out: Xat yozildi = The letter was written.

examples: The contract will be signed today.

body.en: Where English says “people do…”, “you can't…” or uses a passive, Uzbek often uses a passive verb with no subject: Bu yerda o'zbekcha gapiriladi = Uzbek is spoken here. Rules and bans use a verbal noun in -sh / -ish + mumkin, mumkin emas or kerak: Chekish mumkin emas = Smoking is not allowed.

body.en: -adigan (-ydigan after a vowel) turns a verb into an adjective that goes before the noun, for something habitual, possible or still to come: ishlaydigan odam = a person who works, o'qiydigan kitob = a book to read. English needs “who / that / which” or “to + verb”; Uzbek simply puts the verb form in front of the noun.

Where English strings pronouns together (give it to you), Uzbek keeps each one as a separate word with its own case ending: uni (it / him / her, direct object), senga (to you), unga (to him / to her). Time words usually come first and the verb always comes last: Ertaga uni senga beraman = I'll give it to you tomorrow. A pronoun that is obvious is often left out.

body.en: A causative suffix means “make someone do” or “have something done”: o'qimoq (to read, to study) → o'qitmoq (to teach); bilmoq (to know) → bildirmoq (to let know, to inform); qurmoq (to build) → qurdirmoq (to have something built). It is -t- after a vowel and usually -tir- / -dir- after a consonant. English uses make / let / have + verb, or a different verb altogether.

“Would do” is formed with the -(a)r form of the verb + edi: borardim = I would go, qilardim = I would do. In an “if” sentence the condition takes -sa: Vaqtim bo'lsa, borardim = If I had time, I would go. “Could” is -a olardi: yordam bera olardim = I could help.

examples: If I had time, I would go.

title.en: The reason for a feeling: -gani uchun

body.en: To say “I'm glad that…” or “I'm sorry that…”, Uzbek turns the cause into a verbal noun (-gan + possessive) and adds uchun (because of) or a case ending; the feeling comes last: Kelganing uchun xursandman = I'm glad you came; Kasal bo'lganingdan afsusdaman = I'm sorry you're sick.

Uzbek marks “oneself” and “each other” inside the verb. Reflexive -(i)n-: yuvmoq (to wash) → yuvinmoq (to wash oneself). Reciprocal -(i)sh-: ko'rmoq (to see) → ko'rishmoq (to see each other), yozmoq (to write) → yozishmoq (to write to each other). English adds “each other”, or nothing: Ertaga ko'rishamiz = See you tomorrow.

examples: We write to each other often.

body.en: Many shades of meaning come from a main verb in -ib followed by a helper verb: olib kelmoq (take + come = to bring), aytib bermoq (say + give = to tell, for someone), o'qib chiqmoq (read + go out = to read to the end). The helper verb adds direction, completion or doing something for someone else; English often uses a different verb or a particle instead (bring, read through).

Uzbek uses many fixed formulas: Xush kelibsiz (welcome), Yoqimli ishtaha (enjoy your meal), Omad tilayman (good luck), Bayramingiz muborak (happy holiday), Tabriklayman (congratulations). Most of them use the polite siz form, because they are said to guests and elders.

body.en: Official Uzbek prefers set verbs and the passive: murojaat qilmoq (to apply to, to contact), taqdim etmoq (to submit), to'ldirilishi kerak (must be filled in). Instructions use the polite imperative in -(i)ng (to'ldiring, kuting) or a verbal noun + kerak: Hujjatni taqdim etish kerak = It is necessary to submit the document. Officials always address you with siz.

examples: It is necessary to submit the document.

body.en: Start with Kechirasiz (excuse me), say what the problem is with … bor, and ask with the polite “could you…?” form -(i)b bera olasizmi?: Kechirasiz, bir muammo bor = Excuse me, there's a problem; Tekshirib bera olasizmi? = Could you check it for me? To ask for someone higher up: Mas'ul shaxs bilan gaplashmoqchiman.

lines.en: Good afternoon, I'm listening.
I'd like to renew my residence permit.
Do you have the completed form?
Yes, and a copy of the passport too.
The payment receipt is missing.
Can I pay here?
At counter 4. Then come back to me. (formal)
OK, thank you for your patience. (formal)
